note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: tree depth at most 90 levels (JSON nesting stays below 200)
clarifyingQuestions: Should the result be one string or a list of tokens?
Are closing tags required, or only the pre-order tag names?
Can the tree be deep enough to overflow recursion?
hints: Every node contributes exactly two tokens.
The close token is emitted only after every child is finished: that is the DFS post-visit.
Use an explicit stack holding (node, next child index) so deep trees cannot overflow the call stack.
invariants: the stack holds exactly the open, not yet closed, tags from the root down
the output length is 2 * number of nodes
chooseWhen: Trees may be deep and the language has a small recursion limit
tradeoffs: An explicit stack is longer to write than recursion but has no depth limit
hack2hire:685b15536d39467927d2f285.variantLabel: Inferred: open/close tag token list in DFS order

constraints: up to 20000 records, each at most 80 printable ASCII characters
ids [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,10}; names [A-Za-z0-9 _-]{1,20}; no commas inside fields
clarifyingQuestions: In which order are siblings displayed?
What does one output line look like?
Can a child be listed before its parent?
hints: Records can arrive in any order, so read them all before printing anything.
Group children by parent id while keeping record order.
Walk the forest with an explicit stack, pushing children in reverse so the first child is printed first.
invariants: children[p] lists the subtasks of p in record order
a line is printed only after its parent line
chooseWhen: Records are unordered and the hierarchy is wide or deep
tradeoffs: Recursion is simpler but limited in depth; a stack avoids that
hack2hire:6ad141cb7cb0eaedae659263.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: indented forest from task records

constraints: up to 20000 records, each at most 80 printable ASCII characters
ids [A-Za-z0-9_]{1,10}; names [A-Za-z0-9 _-]{1,20}; no commas inside fields
clarifyingQuestions: In which order are siblings displayed?
What does one output line look like?
Can a child be listed before its parent?
Is a parent complete when all its subtasks are?
Can a completion record precede the task definition?
hints: Completion of a parent depends on its children, so compute it bottom-up.
A post-order traversal visits children before parents.

clarifyingQuestions: Is the tower circular like Gas Station?
May the player stop early to avoid negative layers?
Does a reward refill energy?
hints: From a fixed start the stopping layer is the first point where the cost prefix exceeds the energy.
Moving the start down never moves the stopping layer up, because costs are non-negative.
Keep a running cost and point sum over the window [start, stop) and slide both ends.
invariants: window cost <= initialEnergy
stop(s) is non-decreasing in s
tradeoffs: Prefix sums plus binary search is an O(n log n) alternative
hack2hire:68f6f36986f7cb4953d40fbc.variantLabel: Inferred: best start in a one-way tower with forced continuation

clarifyingQuestions: Must adjacent cells differ or match?
Which colour does a region without pre-coloured cells get?
What is returned when no colouring exists?
hints: Boundaries split the board into independent regions.
A grid region is bipartite: every cell's colour is fixed once one cell is fixed.
BFS from a pre-coloured cell, alternate colours, and fail when a neighbour already has the same colour.
invariants: colour(r, c) xor colour(r2, c2) = 1 for adjacent non-boundary cells
chooseWhen: Cells are only constrained by their neighbours
tradeoffs: BFS needs a queue of up to M * N cells; parity reasoning needs no queue but still a region scan
hack2hire:68edba975abdefad4f6693e3.variantLabel: Inferred: two-colouring of regions split by boundaries

constraints: up to 10000 messages, each at most 300 printable ASCII characters
every boundary "@" token is well formed
clarifyingQuestions: Is there an "@all" or "@here" token?
What is the output shape?
Are mentions of non-members counted?
hints: Only tokens that begin at a word boundary are mentions.
Collect each message's mentioned members in a set before counting.
Map member ids to positions with a hash map so each mention is O(1).
invariants: each message adds at most 1 to each member
chooseWhen: Messages are short and members are many
tradeoffs: A per-message set costs memory proportional to the mentions in it

clarifyingQuestions: What is the query budget?
Is the final confirming guess required?
May guesses repeat?
hints: Guessing dddd tells you how many times d occurs.
A digit that does not occur is a perfect filler: it can never match.
Probe one position at a time with one candidate digit and filler elsewhere; the answer is 1 exactly when that digit is there.
invariants: counts sum to 4 after phase 1
a filler probe answers 0 or 1
chooseWhen: Each query is expensive and only exact matches are reported
tradeoffs: At most 19 guesses here; adaptive candidate-set strategies can use fewer but cost more computation
hack2hire:68cdc7ec3735a578b6f27eec.variantLabel: Inferred: digit counting then filler probes, as a guess transcript

clarifyingQuestions: What do later responses mean?
Is there a query limit?
What does "First" tell you?
hints: Comparing two queries tells you which one the target is closer to.
Closer to q than to p means the target lies on q's side of their midpoint.
The consistent set stays an interval: alternate querying its two ends, cut at the midpoint and drop the queried end; "Same" pins the midpoint.
invariants: C = [lo, hi] contains target
every answer is consistent with every target in C
chooseWhen: Feedback is relative to the previous query
tradeoffs: Two queries per halving; reusing the previous query as one end can save queries but is harder to reason about
hack2hire:69c84ccb21f6ab4226966c5a.variantLabel: Inferred: hot/cold alternating-endpoint search, as a query transcript

clarifyingQuestions: Is there a call limit?
Does the final CORRECT have to be observed?
What is returned?
hints: Feedback about a guess arrives on the next call.
Repeating the same guess turns the second answer into feedback about it.
Run ordinary binary search with two identical calls per probe.
invariants: lo <= secret <= hi
each round costs exactly 2 calls
chooseWhen: Simplicity matters more than the call count
tradeoffs: Speculative probing can save calls but needs branching

clarifyingQuestions: Is the delay a parameter or part of the server?
Are PENDING answers counted as calls?
hints: With delay k, the answer to a guess arrives k calls later.
Repeating one guess k + 1 times makes the last answer about it.
Each round is a fixed block of k + 1 identical calls followed by an ordinary binary-search update.
invariants: each round costs delay + 1 calls
chooseWhen: The delay is small relative to log(upperBound)
tradeoffs: Pipelining speculative guesses could hide the delay but complicates the state

constraints: review up to 20000 printable ASCII characters
up to 500 mappings; phrase at most 40 characters
clarifyingQuestions: Is matching case-sensitive?
Which phrase wins when two overlap?
Can one phrase map to several categories?
hints: Only word starts can begin a match.
Prefer the longest phrase, so collect every phrase end you pass and keep the last valid one.
A trie lets you test all phrases from one start in a single walk.
invariants: replacements never overlap
text outside replacements is copied unchanged
tradeoffs: Aho-Corasick finds all matches at once but the left-to-right greedy rule only needs a trie walk

clarifyingQuestions: Which free machine gets the job?
Can a machine take a job that starts exactly when its previous job ends?
Do jobs cross midnight?
hints: Convert HHMM to minutes once.
Keep busy machines in a heap by end time and release every machine that has ended before the job starts.
Keep released machine numbers in a second min-heap so the smallest is taken first.
invariants: every machine is in exactly one heap
machine count = maximum overlap so far
tradeoffs: Two heaps are needed because the release order (end time) differs from the choice order (number)
